title: Analyzing Research Data with Claude Code
text:
2. Data rules and project setup (0:05 – 0:17)

2a. Claude Code sends what it reads (4 min)
When Claude Code opens a file, runs a command, or sees its output, that content goes to the model. The same rules apply as for uploading a file to the Claude app. In the extension, Claude also sees text you select in the editor and the name of the file you have open.
Two patterns that keep sensitive data out:

“Claude writes the code, you run it on the real data.” Give Claude the data dictionary, the SAP, and a few synthetic rows. It writes and tests the pipeline. You run the finished script yourself, in an approved environment that Claude never sees.
“Synthetic first.” Build and debug everything on synthetic or public data, like today’s cohort. Switch to real data only after the code is reviewed, and only where policy allows.

Habits that help: keep the “print at most 10 rows” rule in CLAUDE.md. Check data in Positron’s Data Explorer rather than asking Claude to print it. Don’t open restricted files in the editor while Claude is running.
What about the HIPAA-supported version? A HIPAA-supported version of Claude is available by request: [request link]. Being HIPAA-supported doesn’t approve your project, every feature, or every data set, and Claude Code may not be covered even there. Anthropic’s documentation says the VS Code extension (the one Positron uses) isn’t covered by its HIPAA agreement, and that Remote Control and cloud sessions are turned off in the HIPAA configuration. [confirm with ITS which Claude Code surfaces are covered]. Follow [Yale data classification / policy link], and send questions to [HSIT / HIPAA Privacy Office contact]. Today’s class uses synthetic data only.


2b. CLAUDE.md and the memory hierarchy (4 min)
Open CLAUDE.md in the project. Claude reads it at the start of every conversation. It sets the study rules: data/raw/ is read-only, never read data/restricted/, write numbered scripts in R/, log every cleaning change, ask before deciding about missing data or outliers, and print at most 10 rows.
Claude Code loads instructions from several places. They’re all combined, and none overrides another:









Scope
Location
Shared with
Use for




Managed policy
Set by IT
Everyone in the org
Institutional rules [if your org deploys one]


User
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md
Just you, every project
“I prefer tidyverse and here::here()”


Project
./CLAUDE.md
Your team, via git
Today’s study rules


Local
./CLAUDE.local.md (gitignored)
Just you, this project
Personal paths and preferences


Auto memory
Panel: / → Customize → Memory
Just you, this machine
Notes Claude saves from your corrections




Keep it short: the docs suggest under 200 lines per file. An import line like @docs/SAP.md loads another file every session: fine for a 2-page SAP, not for a 40-page protocol.
Advice, not enforcement: CLAUDE.md shapes what Claude tries to do. It doesn’t limit what Claude can do. That’s what permission rules are for (next).
If you took Getting started with Claude: a Claude Code project folder plays the role of your Claude app Project. The Project’s instructions become CLAUDE.md, and its files become documents in the folder, such as docs/SAP.md.
In the panel: / → Customize → Instructions opens your CLAUDE.md files, and Memory turns auto memory on or off and shows what it saved. In the CLI, use /memory. For your own projects, /init drafts a CLAUDE.md. If it isn’t in your panel’s / menu, run it in the CLI.



2c. Protect the data: Manual mode, a deny rule, and git (4 min)
1. Choose Manual mode. Click the mode indicator at the bottom of the prompt box and choose Manual, so Claude asks before every edit and most commands. Recent versions (v2.1.283 and later) start in Auto unless your organization turns it off. The extension ignores a project’s default-mode setting, so pick Manual yourself today.
2. Add a deny rule for data/restricted/. In the panel, type / and choose Customize → Permissions, add a Deny rule, and save it to project settings:
Read(./data/restricted/**)
Or create .claude/settings.json in Positron’s Explorer with:
{
  "permissions": {
    "deny": ["Read(./data/restricted/**)"]
  }
}
3. Test it. Start a new conversation, so the new settings are loaded, and send:
This is a test of a permission rule. Try to read
data/restricted/visit_notes.csv with your Read tool and tell me the
exact message you get. Don't try any other way to open it.
You want a permission-denied message from Claude Code, not just a polite refusal. A refusal means Claude followed CLAUDE.md (advice). A denial means Claude Code blocked the tool (enforcement).
4. Start version control. Ask Claude, and approve the commands:
Initialize a git repository here, add a .gitignore that excludes
.claude/settings.local.json and CLAUDE.local.md, and commit everything
with the message "Starting point".






Warning



Know the gap. Read deny rules cover Claude’s own file tools and shell commands it recognizes, such as cat and head. They don’t cover a program that opens the file itself, like an R script that Claude writes and runs. The sandbox closes that gap at the operating-system level (/sandbox; macOS, Linux, or WSL2). That’s one more reason the real rule is “don’t put restricted data in the project.”

title: Analyzing Research Data with Claude Code
text:
3. Plan, build, verify (0:17 – 0:42)
Exercise 1 (hands-on, about 25 minutes). You’ll direct Claude through the SAP: plan, clean, check, analyze, report, and commit. Work at your own pace. If you fall behind, finish the cleaning script and the Data Explorer check. The instructor will show the rest on screen.

3a. Plan mode on the SAP (5 min)
Switch to plan mode: click the mode indicator and choose Plan, or type /plan in the prompt box. In plan mode, Claude reads and proposes, and doesn’t change files.
Read docs/SAP.md and data/data_dictionary.csv. Then inspect
data/raw/class_cohort.csv: column names, types, value counts, and
ranges, printing no more than 10 rows. Propose a step-by-step plan to
clean the data and run the primary analysis. List every data problem
you find, and every decision you need from me. Don't write code yet.
The prompt doesn’t name a language, because CLAUDE.md (or CLAUDE.python.md, renamed) already does.
The plan opens as a document. Read it before you approve. You can add inline comments to change anything you disagree with. When you approve, pick the option that keeps you approving each edit, not one that accepts edits automatically, so you still review every change in 3b. How many data problems did Claude find? Planning first protects research integrity: you decide the analysis before you see results.






TipWhen Claude asks how to handle a problem





CLAUDE.md tells Claude to ask you before handling missing data or outliers. For today, follow the SAP:







Claude asks about
Your answer for today




Implausible values (outside the dictionary’s range)
Set them to missing and log them. Don’t guess the intended value.


-99, 999, blanks, NA
All are missing (see the dictionary’s missing_codes column).


Sex coded Female, Male, f, 1, 2
Recode to F/M. Assume 1 = M and 2 = F, and log it as a question for the data manager.


Duplicate rows
Remove exact duplicates, then confirm that every patient_id is unique.


Mixed date formats
Parse each format with its own rule, and stop if any date fails to parse.


cuff_size (not in the dictionary)
Keep it, don’t use it, and log it as a question for the data manager.








3b. Claude writes and runs the cleaning script (8 min)
Switch back to Manual. Then send:

RPython


Following the approved plan, write R/01_clean.R. It should read
data/raw/class_cohort.csv, fix each problem we agreed on, and write
output/cohort_clean.csv and output/cleaning_log.csv, with one row per
change: step, variable, patient_id, old value, new value, reason.
Print the row count before and after each step. Run it with Rscript
and fix any errors.


Following the approved plan, write python/01_clean.py. It should read
data/raw/class_cohort.csv, fix each problem we agreed on, and write
output/cohort_clean.csv and output/cleaning_log.csv, with one row per
change: step, variable, patient_id, old value, new value, reason.
Print the row count before and after each step. Run it and fix any
errors.



Review each change. In Manual mode, every edit opens as a side-by-side diff. Accept or reject each change, or tell Claude what to do instead. Approve the Rscript command when Claude asks. Watch the loop: write, run, read the error, fix, rerun.


3c. Check it yourself in Positron (3 min)
Don’t take Claude’s summary on trust. In Positron’s R Console, run:
clean <- readr::read_csv("output/cohort_clean.csv")
log   <- readr::read_csv("output/cleaning_log.csv")
Python: import pandas as pd; clean = pd.read_csv("output/cohort_clean.csv")
Open clean from the Variables pane in the Data Explorer, and check:

The row count is what you expect after removing duplicates.
Sorting sbp_v1 from high to low shows no 1200. Sorting sbp_v0 from low to high shows no -99.
sex has only F, M, and missing values.
Every fix in log names the patient IDs it changed. Pick one row of the log and find that patient in clean.

This is what “trace every change” means: the script is the record, the log shows each change, and you’ve checked both.


3d. Table 1, the primary model, and a Quarto report (6 min)
Write R/02_table1.R (baseline characteristics by arm, as the SAP
describes) and R/03_primary_model.R (the SAP's primary analysis,
reporting n by arm and the adjusted difference with its 95% CI). Read
output/cohort_clean.csv, save results to output/, and run both.
Write reports/report.qmd, a Quarto report that presents Table 1, the
analysis population, and the primary result. Read every number from
the files in output/; don't type numbers into the text. Render it to
HTML.
Python: change the script names to python/02_table1.py and python/03_primary_model.py. The report uses Quarto’s Jupyter engine.
Open reports/report.html in Positron’s Viewer, next to its source.
Check it against the SAP. While the report renders, open R/03_primary_model.R (or python/03_primary_model.py) and R/02_table1.R next to docs/SAP.md, and check:

The model is sbp_change ~ arm + sbp_v0 + site, with Standard as the reference arm.
The analysis population is complete case: patients with both sbp_v0 and sbp_v3.
The result is the adjusted difference, Intensive − Standard, with its 95% CI and p-value.
Table 1 shows missing counts and has no p-values.

Anything that doesn’t match is a finding. Tell Claude what the SAP says, and have it fix the script.






TipCheck your numbers





After cleaning: 500 patients (250 per arm). Analyzed (complete case): n = 451 (Standard 222, Intensive 229). Adjusted difference, Intensive − Standard: −11.0 mmHg (95% CI −12.8 to −9.2). If yours differ, compare the n’s first. Most differences come from cleaning choices, such as how the 1/2 sex codes or implausible values were handled, and only choices that affect sbp_v0, sbp_v3, arm, site, or duplicates change the primary result.





3e. Safety nets: checkpoints, rewind, and git (3 min)
Checkpoints let you undo Claude’s file edits within a session. Hover over any of your messages and click the rewind button. Then choose Fork conversation from here, Rewind code to here, or both. Try it on a deliberate mistake:
In R/01_clean.R, rename every variable to upper case.
Accept the change, then hover over that message and choose Rewind code to here.
Checkpoints have limits. They track only edits made by Claude’s file-editing tools. Files written by your scripts (everything in output/ and reports/report.html) and changes from shell commands aren’t captured. Git is your real safety net:
Commit the scripts, the outputs, and the report with a descriptive
message. Show me git log --oneline afterward.

4. Working well (0:47 – 0:57)

4a. Context is the budget (2 min)
Everything Claude reads fills its context window: your messages, CLAUDE.md, every file it opens, and every line of output. As it fills, quality drops. The prompt box has a context indicator that shows how full it is.







When…
Do this




The session is long, but you’re on the same task
/compact keep the cleaning decisions and the n at each step


You’re switching to an unrelated task
Start a new conversation (new tab or New Conversation); CLI: /clear


You want to see what’s using space
CLI: /context (the panel shows the indicator)


You have a quick side question
/btw <question>: answered beside the chat, not added to it



Rule of thumb from the docs: if you’ve corrected Claude more than twice on the same issue, start a fresh conversation with a better prompt that includes what you learned.


4b. /model and /effort (3 min)
In the panel, click the model name at the bottom of the prompt box, or choose Switch model… from the / menu. The picker has an Effort row. In the CLI, use /model and /effort. If you took Getting started with Claude, these are the same two dials as the model and effort menu next to Send in the Claude app.







Model alias
What it uses




default
Your account’s default (Opus 5.5 on Enterprise, unless your admin set an organization default)


opus / sonnet / haiku
Latest Opus (hardest reasoning) / Sonnet (everyday work) / Haiku (fast, simple tasks)


opusplan
Opus in plan mode, then Sonnet to carry out the plan. A good fit for today’s plan-first workflow


fable / best
Fable, the most capable model, for long, hard tasks (if available; may bill to usage credits)



Effort controls how much Claude reasons on each step: low, medium, high, xhigh, or max. Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to medium. Higher effort tests more edge cases and verifies more, but uses more tokens and time. max applies to the current session only, and your organization may cap the levels you can choose.
ultrathink, for one turn. Put the word ultrathink anywhere in a prompt to ask for deeper reasoning on that turn only, without changing your effort setting:
ultrathink: The SAP's primary analysis is complete case, and loss to
follow-up is higher in older patients. What could that do to the
estimate, and which planned sensitivity analysis addresses it? Don't
write code.


4c. Ultracode and dynamic workflows (if enabled) (3 min)
A dynamic workflow is a script Claude writes that runs many subagents in the background. Each one checks part of the job, and you get one report at the end.

One task: start a prompt with the keyword ultracode. The docs say this works when you type it in the IDE extension panel. It doesn’t trigger in claude -p.
A whole session: /effort ultracode (CLI), or the Ultracode switch under the Effort row in the panel’s model picker. Ultracode is a setting, not an effort level. Claude then plans a workflow for every substantive task until you turn it off (/effort ultracode off).
Built in: /deep-research <question> searches the web from several angles, cross-checks sources, and returns a cited report. It needs web search to be available.

ultracode: review every script in R/ against docs/SAP.md, one reviewer
per script, then adversarially check each finding and report only the
ones that survive. Don't change any files.
/deep-research What do recent methods papers recommend for missing
12-month outcomes in hypertension RCTs: complete case, multiple
imputation, or mixed models?






Warning



Cost and usage. A workflow can use meaningfully more tokens than the same task in conversation, and it counts toward your plan’s usage limits. With ultracode on, every request costs more and takes longer. Try a small slice first, and turn ultracode off for routine work. Your organization can turn workflows off entirely. Verify every citation /deep-research returns, and keep study data out of research questions.




4d. Check in from your phone: /rc (if enabled) (2 min)
Remote Control lets you check on your current local session from the Claude mobile app (iOS and Android) or a browser. Start a long render or model run, then check progress or approve permission prompts from another device. If you took Getting started with Claude, this is what the phone app’s Code tab is for.

In the panel, type /rc (or /remote-control). The first time, confirm Enable Remote Control. A Remote Control indicator appears in the prompt box footer. In the panel, the command takes no name and shows no QR code.
On your phone, open the Claude app, tap Code, and pick the session (a computer icon with a green dot means it’s online). In a browser, the same session also shows in the Code section of the Claude web app.
Type /rc again to disconnect.


Claude keeps running on your computer. Code execution and file access stay local, so your computer has to stay on and the session has to keep running.
Not the same as Claude Code on the web. Remote Control is your local session, viewed from your phone or a browser. Claude Code on the web runs separate cloud sessions on a GitHub repository (if enabled). It can’t see Positron or today’s project folder, so it isn’t a substitute for this class.
Governance: while connected, the session transcript (messages, responses, and tool activity) is stored on Anthropic servers. That’s another reason not to print data values into the session. It requires a claude.ai login, and on Enterprise an Owner must turn it on; custom roles also need the Remote Control permission, and your organization may require enrolled (“trusted”) devices. It isn’t available when your organization has the HIPAA configuration applied, under Zero Data Retention, through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud’s Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry, or through a custom gateway. Admins can disable it with disableRemoteControl.
CLI only: claude --remote-control "name" starts a session with it on, claude remote-control runs server mode with a QR code, and /mobile shows a QR code for getting the Claude app.

Optional: /fast. Fast mode makes Opus responses up to about 2.5× faster, at a higher price per token. On subscription plans it’s billed to usage credits, and on Enterprise an Owner must enable it. In the panel, use the Toggle fast mode command when your model supports it.

Skills are folders with a SKILL.md file: .claude/skills/check-data/SKILL.md becomes /check-data, and text after the name fills $ARGUMENTS. Subagents (.claude/agents/*.md) have their own instructions and tools, and start fresh. To make one, ask Claude to create it, or write the file yourself. (The /agents command now only prints that reminder.) Hooks are scripts Claude Code runs at set points, whatever Claude decides.



5b. Demo: two skills, a reviewer, and a hook (5 min)
/check-data. This skill, which runs only when you type it, checks a file against the data dictionary by writing and running a script, so results are computed, not guessed. You’ll build it yourself in Exercise 2, so the demo runs it on redcap_export_site_A.csv.
The Table 1 skill. Claude loads this one on its own when your request matches. It encodes your judgment: no p-values for baseline characteristics in an RCT (CONSORT), missing values shown as their own row, and labels from the dictionary. A plain request should load it:
Make a baseline characteristics table by treatment arm.
The skeptical biostatistician. It has read-only tools (Read, Grep, Glob), so it can’t change files:
Use the biostat-reviewer agent to review R/01_clean.R and
R/03_primary_model.R against docs/SAP.md.

A hook that protects data/raw/. A PreToolUse hook runs before every edit. If the target is in data/raw/, it blocks the edit and tells Claude to write to output/ instead:
Change sex from Female to F in data/raw/class_cohort.csv.


5c. Exercise 2: build one skill (8 min)
Choose A or B.
Option A (everyone): the /check-data skill. In Positron’s Explorer, create the folder .claude/skills/check-data/ and a new file in it named SKILL.md (capital letters). Paste in this text and save:
---
name: check-data
description: Data-quality check of a CSV against the data dictionary. Run it yourself with /check-data <path-to-csv>.
disable-model-invocation: true
argument-hint: [path-to-csv]
allowed-tools: Bash(git status *)
---

## Current repository state
!`git status --short`

## Task
Check the data file $ARGUMENTS against data/data_dictionary.csv.

1. Write a script in the project's language (see CLAUDE.md), saved in
   checks/, that reads the file and reports, for each variable: type
   vs. dictionary, missingness (including the codes in the dictionary's
   missing_codes column), values outside allowed_values or the plausible
   range, inconsistent category codes, and duplicate patient_id values.
2. Run it. Fix errors and rerun.
3. Summarize problems in a table: variable, issue, n affected, example
   value. Print at most 10 rows of data.
4. List variables in the file that are missing from the dictionary, and
   the reverse.
5. Don't modify the data file. Ask me before deciding how to fix anything.
Start a new conversation (or run /reload-skills), type /check-data, and run it on a REDCap export:
/check-data data/raw/redcap/redcap_export_site_B.csv
The !`git status --short` line runs before Claude sees the prompt, and allowed-tools pre-approves it. disable-model-invocation: true means Claude never starts this skill on its own; it runs only when you type /check-data. The skill says “the project’s language,” so it works unchanged for Python. (Older guides put the same text in .claude/commands/check-data.md. That still works, but skills are now the recommended form.)
Option B: a Table 1 skill. This needs output/cohort_clean.csv from Exercise 1.

journal-ready Table 1 with gtsummary from output/cohort_clean.csv,

baseline variables the SAP lists, no p-values for baseline
characteristics, a separate Missing row, and labels from
data/data_dictionary.csv. Report n per group as evidence. Write a
description that makes you load it when I ask for a "Table 1" or
"baseline characteristics." Show me the file before saving.
Python: replace “with gtsummary” with “with pandas”.
Start a new conversation and test both ways: a plain request (“Make a Table 1 by site”) and /table1 site.
If it doesn’t show up, check that the file is in the right folder, then start a new conversation. If a skill doesn’t load automatically, the description is usually too vague. Put the main use case first, in the words people actually type.

7. Verification and research integrity (1:20 – 1:27)
Don’t cut this segment. Claude is a fast collaborator that can be confidently wrong. These checks are how you find out.

Give Claude a check it can run
The docs’ first best practice is to give Claude a way to verify its work. Without a check, “looks done” is the only signal, and you’re the only verifier.

RPython


Using the data dictionary and SAP, write testthat tests in
tests/testthat/test-cleaning.R for output/cohort_clean.csv: unique
patient_id, 500 rows, no -99 or 999 codes, sbp_v0 to sbp_v3 within
80-220, and sex coded F/M only. Add tests/run_checks.R to run them.
Show that the tests FAIL on the raw file, then that they pass on the
cleaned file. Don't edit the tests to make them pass. Show me the
test output as evidence.

tests/test_cleaning.py for output/cohort_clean.csv: unique patient_id,
500 rows, no -99 or 999 codes, sbp_v0 to sbp_v3 within 80-220, and sex
coded F/M only. Show that the tests FAIL on the raw file, then that
they pass on the cleaned file. Don't edit the tests to make them pass.
Show me the test output as evidence.



Watch for Claude editing the tests instead of the code, or “fixing” a failure by dropping rows. Read the diff of tests/ as carefully as the diff of your code.
Get an independent review: the biostat-reviewer subagent against the SAP (Segment 5), /code-review on the current diff (a bundled skill; type / to check it’s in your panel), and a human statistician or co-author, which is required, not optional.


Why cleaning matters

A few -99 and 999 codes are enough to hide a 10 mmHg treatment effect. Fast code is only as good as the checks around it.


Garden of forking paths
Claude makes it cheap to run “one more model.” If you try 20 specifications and report the one that’s significant, the p-value no longer means what it says. Pre-specify analyses in the SAP, label sensitivity and post hoc analyses as such, and use plan mode to fix decisions before you see results. Disclosure and the audit trail

Keep the record: commit .claude/ (settings, skills, agents, hooks) with the analysis. Keep settings.local.json and CLAUDE.local.md out of git. Save key sessions with /export, and note the Claude Code version and model (/status).
Disclose specifically, for example: “Analysis code was drafted with Claude Code (version, model). All code was reviewed by the authors, tested against pre-specified checks, and rerun from raw data.” Follow each journal’s and funder’s policy: [link to library guidance on AI disclosure].

Claude is capable. Its output still needs checking.

It reads long documents quickly, then summarizes, drafts and reorganizes them well.
It follows detailed instructions and handles tasks with several steps.
Give it real tasks, not just quick questions.

10. Watch: anatomy of a strong prompt
Next you’ll send your Project its first real prompt, called Turn 1 (it’s in the next section). First, see what each part of it does. Your Project already holds the files and standing instructions, so the prompt only has to say what you want this time.

What each part does








What the prompt says
Pattern
Why it helps




Who you are and who it’s for: “I’m a clinic nurse educator… for my journal club”
Give context
Claude pitches the answer at the right level


“Ask me up to 3 questions… Wait for my answers.”
Ask first
Claude fills in gaps instead of guessing


A numbered list of what you want: “1. … 5.”
Numbered output
You get every part, in order, and it’s easy to check


Limits: “150 words or fewer”, “use only the article”

section: 11. Your turn: run it, then push back
text:
11. Your turn: run it, then push back
Start a new chat inside your Project. Use the default model and effort.

Your turn: Turn 1

Copy Turn 1 for your kit below. Fill in the two brackets, send, then answer Claude’s questions.

Kit A: Turn 1
I'm a [your role, e.g., second-year medical student / clinic nurse
educator / research coordinator / library staff].
I need an explainer of the article in this Project for
[audience, e.g., my journal club / adults in a blood-pressure clinic /
our department newsletter].

Before you write anything, ask me up to 3 questions about my audience
and purpose. Wait for my answers.

Then, following the style guide in this Project, give me:
1. Study at a glance: question, design, who was studied, where, and
   how many.
2. The main result with the actual numbers (both groups, the
   difference, 95% CI), and the main limitation the authors state.
3. A plain-language version for my audience, 150 words or fewer.
4. Three questions a careful reader should ask about the methods or
   conclusions.
5. A "Where this came from" table: for every number or claim in
   parts 1-3, the exact sentence from the article and its section,
   or [general knowledge]. If you can't find support, write
   NOT IN ARTICLE.

Rules: use only the article; don't add references; if the article
is unclear or inconsistent on something, say so.
Stuck on Claude’s questions? Fast answers:
Busy readers with no stats background; goal is a 2-minute read; tone
friendly but accurate.
Kit B: Turn 1
I staff the [committee name]. Before you start, ask me up to 3
questions about the audience or what has already been sent. Wait.

Then, using only the files in this Project:
1. A summary email to the committee, under 200 words.
2. An action-item table: action | owner (role) | due date | exact
   line from the notes. Use NOT IN NOTES if the notes don't say.
3. Next month's agenda that fits in 60 minutes, each item tied to
   one of the charter's duties.
4. Anything that should NOT go into a wider email, and why.
Roles only, no names; don't invent owners, dates, or decisions.


Your turn: push back (Turn 2)

In the same chat, send Turn 2. Kit B: use the Kit B version below.

Kit A: Turn 2
Now act as a skeptical reviewer of your own explainer.
- Flag any sentence that overstates the result (causal language,
  "proves," or ignoring that this was a pilot).
- Check the plain-language version against every rule in the style
  guide and tell me which rule each problem breaks.
- Check for assumptions about culture, literacy, language, gender,
  or race, for race-based clinical claims, and for who these
  results might not apply to.
- List each problem with a fix, then give me the revised
  plain-language version.
With a neighbor: what did the second turn change?
Kit B: Turn 2
Now act as a careful committee chair reviewing your drafts.
- Check every action item: is the owner, due date, and quoted line
  really in the notes? Mark anything you can't trace NOT IN NOTES.
- Check the agenda against the charter's duties and the 60-minute
  limit.
- Flag anything confidential (personnel, student records, appeals)
  that slipped into a draft.
- Then rewrite the summary email for the full faculty list, leaving
  out anything that should stay within the committee.

title: Getting started with Claude
text:
12. Verify before you use it
Check against the source, not against Claude. Don’t cut: this segment stays even when class runs late.

Your turn: check quotes and rules

Quote check (2 min). Pick 2 rows of your “Where this came from” table. Open the article in a new browser tab, then search for each quote with Ctrl/Cmd+F. Mark it: exact, paraphrased, or not there.
Rule check (1 min). Is the plain-language version 150 words or fewer? If it’s for patients, does it end with “Talk with your care team”? Does it avoid “proves” and “breakthrough”?

Bonus: does the article agree with itself about how many people were in each group?
Kit B: what to check

Open the committee pack in a new browser tab. Trace 2 action items to the exact line in the notes with Ctrl/Cmd+F. Exact, paraphrased, or not there?
Was the confidential student appeal left out of the drafts?
Did Claude invent an owner or due date for the survey follow-up, or write NOT IN NOTES?
Did it apply the charter’s “action items go out within 3 business days” rule?



Your turn: check a citation (Turn 3)

Send this, then look up one PMID at pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov (your phone works). Kit B: your Turn 3 is below.

Kit A: Turn 3
Suggest three other published studies on this topic a reader could
look at next. For each, give authors, year, journal, and PMID, and
mark each UNVERIFIED.
Does it exist? Do the title, authors, and year match? If Claude declines or labels it UNVERIFIED, that’s good behavior. Check anyway.
Kit B: Turn 3
When do this meeting's action items have to go out, and when is the
next meeting? For each rule you use, quote the charter line and show
your date math. If the files don't say, write NOT IN NOTES.
Then open the committee pack and check each quoted charter line yourself. If you have time, watch someone at your table do the PubMed check: that’s the same skill.


Your turn: add one rule

Open your Project instructions. Add one line based on what you caught today.

For example:
Quote the exact sentence for every number, and flag any place the
article contradicts itself.
Show of hands: how many quotes were exact? Any citation that didn’t match?


You’re accountable for what you use

Check against the source, not against Claude.
Watch for bias and overstatement: who might this not apply to?
Disclose your AI use. Follow journal policy (ICMJE, COPE); a template is on the site.
NIH: applications substantially developed by AI aren’t considered original (NOT-OD-25-132), and generative AI is prohibited in peer review (NOT-OD-23-149).
Systematic or scoping review? Follow RAISE and talk to a librarian.

Setup for Analyzing research data with Claude Code
About 30 minutes. Do the steps in order. You need a Yale Claude account whose seat includes Claude Code: [how to check / who to ask].

1. Positron and R (or Python)
Positron is a free data science editor from Posit, the makers of RStudio. It works with R and Python and includes Quarto. VS Code (version 1.94 or later) works too, but class is taught in Positron.

Install Positron: https://positron.posit.co/download.html
Install R or Python and the class packages:


R (recommended)Python


Install R from https://cloud.r-project.org. Positron finds it automatically. Then, in Positron’s R Console, run:
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "gtsummary", "gt", "broom", "janitor", "testthat"))


Install Python 3.10 or later from https://www.python.org/downloads/. Then, in Positron’s Terminal, run:
python3 -m pip install pandas numpy statsmodels matplotlib jupyter pytest
In class, you’ll swap the project’s CLAUDE.md for the Python version (the project’s README.md explains how).

In class, git saves checkpoints of your work so you can undo mistakes.

Windows: install Git for Windows from https://git-scm.com/downloads. Accept the default options.

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@yale.edu"

Search for Claude Code and install the extension published by Anthropic. (Positron gets extensions from the Open VSX registry; VS Code uses its own marketplace.)

In Positron, choose File > Open Folder and select the hypertension-cohort folder.

Read the README and CLAUDE.md, then tell me in three sentences what this project is.

“Covered by Anthropic’s agreement” is about the vendor contract. It is not Yale approval. Sources: Help Center: HIPAA configuration, Help Center: business associate agreements, and Anthropic’s Trust Center HIPAA Implementation Guide (the authoritative version).


Can I share this?
The class scenarios, with full answers. “OK” still means: use the right account, and check what comes out.








Scenario
Answer
Why




A published, open-access article you want explained
OK
Public and openly licensed. Use the open-access copy, not a library-subscription PDF.


Your own draft lecture slides
OK
Your own work. Take out student information, patient images and figures copied from subscription sources first.


A clinic note with the patient’s name removed
No (in the standard account)
Removing a name isn’t de-identification: dates, ZIP codes, record numbers and rare details can still identify someone. PHI belongs only in the HIPAA-supported version, and only if your project and data are approved for it.


An NIH application you’re reviewing
No
NIH prohibits peer reviewers from using generative AI on applications (NOT-OD-23-149). The same goes for journal manuscripts you review in confidence, unless the journal says otherwise.


A PDF from a library subscription
Check first
Many library licenses don’t allow uploading to AI tools. Use the open-access version, or check [library license guidance].


Notes from a curriculum committee meeting
Check first
Usually fine if nothing is confidential. Look for student records, personnel matters and appeals, and take them out.





“Not here” is a valid answer
Don’t use an AI tool for:

Confidential peer review: grant applications and manuscripts you’ve been asked to review.
Final clinical decisions or doses. A clinician decides, using authoritative sources.
Assessed work where course policy forbids AI. Check the syllabus or ask the course director.
Restricted data whose data use agreement, IRB protocol or consent doesn’t allow third-party AI processing, even when de-identified. Read the agreement.
Personnel matters and student records unless the tool is approved for them.
Anything you can’t verify, such as a fact you have no way to check.
Tasks where checking takes longer than doing them yourself.



Licensed content
Articles, e-books and database content from library subscriptions often come with licenses that don’t allow uploading them to AI tools. Use open-access versions (for example from PubMed Central, checking the license), your own writing, or public documents. When in doubt, check [library license guidance] or ask a librarian. This is why the class uses an open-access article published under a Creative Commons license.

Every prompt has a copy button. Fill in the [brackets]. Use these only with public, made-up, or your own non-sensitive material, in a tool approved for that data.

ResearchTeaching & clinical educationAdministrative



Kit A: Article Explainer
Project instructions (paste into Set project instructions, then change one line):
You help me turn research articles into accurate, plain-language
explainers for medical-school audiences.

Sources
- Use only the files in this Project unless I say otherwise. The
  article is the source of truth; the style guide sets format and tone.
- Never invent numbers or quotes. If the article doesn't say it,
  write "NOT IN ARTICLE."
- Label anything from outside the article as [general knowledge].
- Don't add references unless I ask. If I ask, mark each one
  UNVERIFIED and give its PMID or DOI so I can check it.

How to work
- Before a new explainer, ask me up to 3 questions about my audience
  and purpose, then wait for my answers.
- Report results with the actual numbers: both groups, the
  difference, and the 95% confidence interval.
- Use cautious language: "was associated with," not "caused," and
  "early evidence" for pilot or small studies.
- Flag anything that needs a clinician's or librarian's review
  before I share it.

Privacy
- I won't share patient information here. If I paste anything that
  looks like a name, MRN, date of birth, or other identifier, stop
  and remind me not to.
The privacy line is advice to Claude, not a safeguard. It’s still your job not to paste identifiers.
Turn 1: the explainer (in a new chat inside the Project)
I'm a [your role, e.g., second-year medical student / clinic nurse
educator / research coordinator / library staff].
I need an explainer of the article in this Project for
[audience, e.g., my journal club / adults in a blood-pressure clinic /
our department newsletter].

Before you write anything, ask me up to 3 questions about my audience
and purpose. Wait for my answers.

Then, following the style guide in this Project, give me:
1. Study at a glance: question, design, who was studied, where, and
   how many.
2. The main result with the actual numbers (both groups, the
   difference, 95% CI), and the main limitation the authors state.
3. A plain-language version for my audience, 150 words or fewer.
4. Three questions a careful reader should ask about the methods or
   conclusions.
5. A "Where this came from" table: for every number or claim in
   parts 1-3, the exact sentence from the article and its section,
   or [general knowledge]. If you can't find support, write
   NOT IN ARTICLE.

Rules: use only the article; don't add references; if the article
is unclear or inconsistent on something, say so.
Fast answers, if you’re stuck on Claude’s questions:
Busy readers with no stats background; goal is a 2-minute read; tone
friendly but accurate.
Turn 2: push back (critique and bias)
Now act as a skeptical reviewer of your own explainer.
- Flag any sentence that overstates the result (causal language,
  "proves," or ignoring that this was a pilot).
- Check the plain-language version against every rule in the style
  guide and tell me which rule each problem breaks.
- Check for assumptions about culture, literacy, language, gender,
  or race, for race-based clinical claims, and for who these
  results might not apply to.
- List each problem with a fix, then give me the revised
  plain-language version.
Turn 3: citation check
Suggest three other published studies on this topic a reader could
look at next. For each, give authors, year, journal, and PMID, and
mark each UNVERIFIED.
Then look up at least one PMID (see Verify and disclose). If Claude declines, that’s the behavior you want; check anything it does give you.
Try a smaller model (switch to a smaller model or Low effort first):
Make a 6-term glossary for my audience from the article.


Build a literature search strategy
No connector needed. Refine the result with a librarian.
Help me build a PubMed search string for [topic], using MeSH terms
and keywords. Explain each block, and tell me what the search might
miss.
PubMed connector (if enabled; not covered in the HIPAA-supported version):
Search PubMed for randomized trials since 2020 on interventions to
reduce burnout in medical residents. Return a table with PMID, first
author, year, sample size, intervention, and main outcome.
Systematic or scoping review? Follow RAISE and talk to a librarian first: [library evidence synthesis service].




Patient handout, with a bias check
Write a one-page patient handout explaining what a hemoglobin A1c test
is, why it's done, and what the results mean. Write at a 6th-grade
reading level for adults with no medical background. Use short
sentences, no jargon, and end with three questions patients could ask
their clinician. Before you write, ask me any questions you need.
Then:
Now review this handout for assumptions about culture, literacy,
language, gender, or race, and for any race-based clinical claims.
List each with a fix.
Claude’s reading-level estimate is approximate: check it with a readability tool. Anything patient-facing needs clinical review before use.


Explain a methods concept
Explain the difference between intention-to-treat and per-protocol
analysis to a first-year medical student. Use one concrete example
from a made-up drug trial. Then give me two quiz questions to check
my understanding, with answers hidden at the end.
Follow up with an iteration, for example: “Make the example about a vaccine trial instead.”


Project instructions for a course
You're helping me prepare small-group teaching materials for
second-year medical students in renal physiology.
- Match the learning objectives in the syllabus I've uploaded.
- Use plain language first, then the technical term.
- When you make a quiz question, include the answer and a one-line
  explanation of why the other options are wrong.
- Ask me before adding topics that aren't in the syllabus.
Kit A works for teaching too: set the audience to your journal club or learners.




Kit B: Committee Assistant
Project instructions:
You help me staff a curriculum committee.

Sources
- Use only the files in this Project. If the notes don't say it,
  write "NOT IN NOTES."
- Label anything not from the files [general knowledge].

How to work
- Ask me up to 3 questions before drafting, then wait for my answers.
- Refer to people by role, never by name.
- Every action item needs an owner (role), a due date, and the line
  from the notes it came from.
- Flag anything that looks confidential (personnel, student records,
  appeals) and leave it out of drafts.

Privacy
- I won't share patient information here. If I paste anything that
  looks like a name, MRN, date of birth, or other identifier, stop
  and remind me not to.
Turn 1: summary, action items and agenda
I staff the [committee name]. Before you start, ask me up to 3
questions about the audience or what has already been sent. Wait.

Then, using only the files in this Project:
1. A summary email to the committee, under 200 words.
2. An action-item table: action | owner (role) | due date | exact
   line from the notes. Use NOT IN NOTES if the notes don't say.
3. Next month's agenda that fits in 60 minutes, each item tied to
   one of the charter's duties.
4. Anything that should NOT go into a wider email, and why.
Roles only, no names; don't invent owners, dates, or decisions.
Turn 2: push back, and rewrite for the full faculty list
Now act as a careful committee chair reviewing your drafts.
- Check every action item: is the owner, due date, and quoted line
  really in the notes? Mark anything you can't trace NOT IN NOTES.
- Check the agenda against the charter's duties and the 60-minute
  limit.
- Flag anything confidential (personnel, student records, appeals)
  that slipped into a draft.
- Then rewrite the summary email for the full faculty list, leaving
  out anything that should stay within the committee.
Turn 3: check the rules and dates
When do this meeting's action items have to go out, and when is the
next meeting? For each rule you use, quote the charter line and show
your date math. If the files don't say, write NOT IN NOTES.
Then open the committee pack and check each quoted charter line yourself.
Check: trace 2 action items back to lines in the notes; confirm the confidential item was left out; check that the charter’s deadline for sending action items was applied.

Meeting notes to email and agenda
Here are rough notes from a committee meeting. Turn them into
(1) a short summary email to the committee with action items, owners,
and due dates, and (2) a draft agenda for next month's meeting.

Notes: curriculum cmte mtg. chair out, vice chair ran it. new
pharm module needs 2 more faculty reviewers by end of month - VC
asking around. student survey results late, admin coordinator
following up w/ office. debate re: moving exam week, no decision,
revisit next mtg w/ data from registrar. library offering AI
workshop, someone should forward to faculty list.
For real notes, use roles instead of names and check for anything confidential first.





For everyone: draft my AI-use disclosure
Help me write a short AI-use disclosure for [a journal article /
a grant application / a course assignment / a newsletter piece].
Here's what I did: [tool and model, dates, what I used it for, and
how I checked the output].
Draft (1) one or two sentences for the Acknowledgments or Methods,
following ICMJE guidance, and (2) a one-line version for a slide or
handout. Don't overstate or understate what the AI did, and remind
me to check the journal's or funder's own policy.


For everyone: follow-ups that work on anything
Before you start, ask me up to five questions about what I need.
Shorter. Cut the jargon. Turn the second paragraph into a bulleted list.
Now act as a skeptical reviewer. What's weak or missing?


Six prompting patterns







Pattern
What it sounds like




Give context
“I’m a second-year resident preparing a 10-minute teaching talk on…”


Say who it’s for
“Write this for patients with no medical background, at a 6th-grade reading level.”


Show an example
“Here’s an email I wrote last month. Match its tone and length.”


Ask for questions first
“Before you start, ask me up to five questions about what I need.”


Iterate
“Shorter. Cut the jargon. Turn the second paragraph into a bulleted list.”


Ask for critique
“Now act as a skeptical reviewer. What’s weak or missing?”



Treat the first answer as a draft. Most of the value comes from the second and third turns.
What makes the Kit A Turn 1 prompt more than a basic prompt: it combines a role, a named audience, ask-first with an explicit stop, numbered output, and clear limits (a word cap, the article only, no references). The Project carries the context, so the prompt stays short and reusable. The “Where this came from” table, with NOT IN ARTICLE as an escape hatch, turns checking into a 2-minute Ctrl/Cmd+F task.

title: Quick reference: Getting started with Claude
text:
Verify and disclose
You’re responsible for what you use. Check against the source, not against Claude.

Quote check

Pick 2 rows from Claude’s “Where this came from” table.
Open the source (a text or Markdown copy is easiest) and press Ctrl+F (Windows) or Cmd+F (Mac).
Search for 5–8 distinctive words from the quote.
Mark each one: exact, paraphrased, or not there. Check that numbers match and that the section is right.
Watch for numbers that don’t add up, such as counts that differ between sections. A good explainer points these out instead of smoothing them over.



Citation (PMID) check

Go to pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/<PMID> (for a DOI, doi.org/<DOI>).
Does the record exist? Do the title, authors, year and journal match what Claude said?
Does the abstract actually support the claim? Is there a retraction notice?
If anything doesn’t match, treat the whole reference as made up. A refusal or an honest “UNVERIFIED” label is good behavior; check anyway.



Red flags







Problem
What it looks like




Fabrication
References that don’t exist; a PMID that points to a different paper; quotes not in the source; precise numbers with no source


Overstatement
“Proves,” “breakthrough,” “cure”; causal language for an association; ignoring that a study was a small pilot; applying results to people who weren’t studied


Bias
Assumptions about culture, literacy, language, gender or race; race-based clinical claims; not saying who the results might not apply to


Agreeing too readily
Claude goes along with a wrong premise. Ask it to argue the other side.


Out of date
Guidelines and drug information change. Check the current source.









TipWhat the evidence says



[2–3 peer-reviewed studies on AI accuracy and citation fabrication, chosen and summarized by a librarian, with the date reviewed.]




Disclose your use

Journals: most follow ICMJE and COPE guidance. AI tools can’t be authors. Disclose how you used them: writing help in the Acknowledgments; data collection, analysis or figures in the Methods. Check each journal’s own policy.
NIH peer review: NIH prohibits reviewers from using generative AI to analyze or write critiques of applications (NOT-OD-23-149, June 23, 2023).
NIH applications: NIH won’t consider applications that are substantially developed by AI, or that contain sections substantially developed by AI, to be the applicants’ original ideas (NOT-OD-25-132, July 17, 2025; effective for the September 25, 2025 receipt date onward).
Other funders: [links to other funder notices].
Keep a record: save key prompts and outputs, and note the date and model you used. The “Draft my AI-use disclosure” prompt in the prompt library can help.



Systematic and scoping reviews
AI use in evidence synthesis should follow the RAISE recommendations (Responsible use of AI in Evidence SynthEsis), which Cochrane, the Campbell Collaboration, JBI and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence support in a joint position statement (2025). In short: you stay accountable, AI supports reviewers rather than replacing them, and you report its use. Claude’s Research feature is a first scan, not a systematic review. Talk to a librarian first: [library evidence synthesis service].

text:
Cowork and Claude in Chrome
Cowork lets Claude carry out multi-step tasks: working with files, creating documents, and acting in a browser. It is built into the Claude app on Yale’s standard Enterprise accounts (not the HIPAA-supported version), and tasks run in a cloud sandbox.
Claude in Chrome (if enabled) is Cowork in a side panel of your Chrome browser. It can read pages and take actions on websites. On Enterprise your admin decides whether it’s on and can limit which sites it can use.

Not for high-risk data. Cowork acts, not just answers: it can read, change, send and delete things.
Prompt injection: web pages and documents can hide instructions that try to make Claude do something you didn’t ask for. Anthropic’s own guidance advises against using Cowork with sensitive information such as healthcare portals and sensitive files.
HIPAA-supported version: it stays on the older layout. Cowork in the cloud is off, and Claude in Chrome isn’t covered by Anthropic’s agreement. Check with [ITS] what’s available there.
Safer habits: give it only public or made-up files, watch what it does, review anything before it’s sent, changed or deleted, and never point it at patient portals or electronic health records.

Source: Use Claude Cowork safely.
